sections.skill: State the output format and constraints a result must meet

questions.domain: Foundation 4: Asking for what you need
questions.prompt: Which part of a request describes the OUTPUT FORMAT?

choices.text: "as a table with Item and Price columns"
"so we can choose a caterer by Friday"

questions.correct_answer: "as a table with Item and Price columns"
questions.intro: Besides saying what you want, say what the result should LOOK LIKE. The OUTPUT FORMAT is its shape: a bulleted list, a table with named columns, a three-paragraph letter, a numbered set of steps. CONSTRAINTS are limits it must respect: a length ("under 150 words"), a tone ("friendly but professional"), a reading level ("for beginners"), or things to avoid ("no jargon," "do not mention prices"). Stating format and constraints up front saves rounds of revision and makes the result easy to check: you can see at once whether it has five bullets or is under 150 words.
questions.feedback: Format is the shape of the result.

sections.skill: Turn a vague wish into a checkable instruction

questions.domain: Foundation 4: Asking for what you need
questions.prompt: Which instruction is checkable?
questions.intro: A CHECKABLE instruction is one you can test by looking at the result. "Short" is vague: short to whom? "Under 100 words" is checkable: count and see. "Nice looking" is vague; "a table with three columns" is checkable. "Friendly" is partly vague, but "no technical terms" is easier to test. To turn a wish into a checkable instruction, ask: "What would I look for to know it was done?" Then write that down as the instruction.
questions.feedback: You can count to check it.

sections.title: Apply it

sections.skill: Check whether constraints were actually followed

questions.domain: Foundation 4: Asking for what you need
questions.prompt: A response says, "Here is your summary in under 100 words," but it looks long. What should you do?

choices.text: Trust the claim, since it said it complied
Ask it to repeat the claim
Assume all summaries are under 100 words

questions.intro: Format and constraints work best when they are specific and checkable. "Keep it short" is vague; "under 100 words" can be checked. "Make it look nice" is vague; "a table with columns Name, Date and Cost" can be checked. Tools do not always follow every constraint, especially exact word counts or many rules at once, so check the result against each one. If a constraint really matters, such as a character limit for a form, verify it yourself rather than trusting the tool's claim that it complied.
questions.feedback: Verify constraints that matter.
